title: Closures and function factories
tasks: dim_lights(level) and blinds_to(position): factories that return routines
chain(*routines): combine routines into one, like a multicast delegate
make_counter() with nonlocal, and make_toggle(device_id) with ROOM_TOGGLES built safely in a loop
PRESETS, preset_uses (one counter each), run_preset(name) and preset_names()
explanation: dim_lights(15) and dim_lights(70) are two different functions because each call to the factory creates a new level variable for its routine to capture. make_counter relies on nonlocal so bump can rebind count. ROOM_TOGGLES goes through make_toggle on purpose: a lambda written directly in the loop would share one variable and every toggle would hit the last room.

hints.title: Factories
hints.content: def dim_lights(level): define an inner def routine(devs) that does apply_to(select(devs.values(), by_kind(Kind.LIGHT)), lambda light: light.execute("dim", level)), then return routine (no parentheses). blinds_to is the same with Kind.BLINDS and "position".

hints.title: State and chaining
hints.content: make_counter: count = 0 outside, def bump(): nonlocal count; count += 1; return count, and return bump. chain(*routines) defines def combined(devs): for routine in routines: routine(devs) and returns combined. make_toggle(device_id) returns a toggle() that flips devices[device_id].

hints.title: Tables
hints.content: ROOM_TOGGLES = {room.value: make_toggle(f"{room.value}_light") for room in Room}. PRESETS maps names to chain(dim_lights(15), blinds_to(0)) and friends. preset_uses = {name: make_counter() for name in PRESETS}; run_preset calls preset_uses[name]() for the count.

checks.prompt:
What does this print?

~~~python
fns = []
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    fns.append(lambda: n)
print([f() for f in fns])
~~~
checks.explanation: Each lambda captures the *variable* `n`, not its value at that moment. After the loop `n` is 3, so every call returns 3. Fix it with a factory, `lambda n=n: n`, or `functools.partial`.

checks.prompt: When is `nonlocal` required inside a closure?

options: Whenever the closure reads an outer variable
When the closure rebinds (assigns to) an outer variable
When the closure calls an outer function
When the closure appends to an outer list

checks.explanation: Reading, calling and mutating (`items.append(...)`) all work without a declaration. Only assignment such as `count += 1` makes Python treat the name as local, so you must say `nonlocal count` to rebind the outer one.
